items.title: Charlie De Vore Interview, 1962-07-04
items.q: I noticed the D does a lot of that with his lip too

ctx.x: Oh no. He was talking just about the way he was holding it. Yeah. Well this... You see now a valve instrument, a trombone player, he can do all sorts of little things. Lissandos because he's got a slime and a valve instrument doesn't. And these are where the real subtlies involved in the music. And I think it would take a young guy playing. I work on that half-valve stuff all the time because I think that's where you can get the real shadings and the meanings and the blues. Anything can play. Lee Collins... I…
I noticed the D does a lot of that with his lip too, not just with his... Yeah.

It's a combination of lip and valves on that. You bend notes. As a matter of fact, I never thought when I'm trying to play that I should hit it right on a button. You know? Hit it above or below to get that bending quality. That gives you the blues sound. A Negro scale has been graphically illustrated as flatting the 3rd and the 7th. You know? But actually it's every note. A Negro scale is so completely African in nature that it hasn't any relationship to a diatonic scale. At first, here it says that's what gives…
